facts.statement: Youngosuchus lived during the Middle Triassic period in China.
facts.quote: Youngosuchus is an extinct genus of archosaur from the Middle Triassic of China.

facts.statement: The type species Youngosuchus sinensis was first described in 1973 as a species of the genus Vjushkovia.
facts.quote: The type species is Y. sinensis. Y. sinensis was first described in 1973 as a new species of the erythrosuchid Vjushkovia.

facts.statement: In 1985, the species was moved from Vjushkovia to its own genus, Youngosuchus.
facts.quote: In 1985, it was reassigned as its own genus of rauisuchid.

facts.statement: The species was originally described in 1973 by the Chinese paleontologist C.C. Young.
facts.quote: The skeleton of Youngosuchus was first described in 1973 by Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian, better known as C.C. Young.

facts.statement: Russian paleontologists Kalandadze and Sennikov established the genus Youngosuchus in 1985, naming it after C.C. Young.
facts.quote: In 1985, Russian paleontologists N.N. Kalandadze and Andreii Sennikov erected Youngosuchus as a new genus for V. sinensis, naming it after Young.

facts.statement: Fossils of Youngosuchus come from the Kelamayi Formation in the Junggur Basin of Xinjiang, China.
facts.quote: Youngosuchus is known from a well-preserved skeleton recovered from the Kelamayi Formation in the Junggur Basin of Xinjiang, China.

facts.statement: The known fossil specimen IVPP V 3239 contains a complete skull, neck vertebrae, ribs, shoulder girdle, and front limbs.
facts.quote: The skeleton, referred to as IVPP V 3239, includes a complete skull, cervical vertebrae, ribs, the pectoral girdle, and forelimbs.

facts.statement: Youngosuchus possessed a large, deep skull equipped with sharp, curved teeth.
facts.quote: Youngosuchus has a large, deep skull with sharp recurved teeth.

facts.statement: The skeleton lacks osteoderms, suggesting Youngosuchus did not have the body armor found in other early archosauriforms.
facts.quote: Osteoderms are not present on the skeleton, a possible indication that Youngosuchus did not have the body armor present in other early archosauriforms.

facts.statement: Recent studies classify Youngosuchus as a rauisuchian-grade loricatan archosaur unrelated to the genus Vjushkovia.
facts.quote: more recent studies classify it as a "rauisuchian"-grade loricatan archosaur completely unrelated to Vjushkovia, which is most likely a synonym of Garjainia.

facts.statement: Rauisuchids, the group to which Youngosuchus was assigned, are more derived than erythrosuchids and belong to the clade Pseudosuchia.
facts.quote: Rauisuchids are more derived than erythrosuchids because they lie within Archosauria, specifically within the clade Pseudosuchia.

facts.statement: The initial classification of Youngosuchus as a rauisuchid was not widely accepted by all paleontologists.
facts.quote: The assignment of Youngosuchus to Rauisuchidae was not widely accepted initially.

facts.statement: Paleontologist J. Michael Parrish argued in 1992 that Youngosuchus sinensis should remain in the genus Vjushkovia, distinct from Garjainia.
facts.quote: Paleontologist J. Michael Parrish kept Y. sinensis as a species of Vjushkovia in his 1992 study of erythrosuchids, and continued to recognize Vjushkovia as a valid taxon distinct from Garjainia.

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Martin Ezcurra suggested Youngosuchus is a close relative of the loricatan Batrachotomus and distinct from Garjainia.
facts.quote: Martin Ezcurra (2016)'s study of archosauromorph classification placed Youngosuchus as a close relative of the loricatan Batrachotomus, positioned far away from Garjainia (which was considered indistinguishable from Vjushkovia).

facts.statement: Youngosuchus belongs to the parent group Pseudosuchia.
